summary: Defines Opus, an audio codec for interactive speech and music. It handles uses such as voice over IP, videoconferencing, in-game chat, and live music, and scales from low-bitrate narrowband speech up to very high quality stereo music. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Opus compresses speech and music for interactive audio, such as voice calls, video conferences, and live music. It combines two coding methods and can change between them as the sound or network conditions change. RFC 8251 later updates the decoder code that defines this specification.

subtitle: A single interactive audio codec combines speech and music coding across a wide range of rates and delays.

tldr.problem: Interactive audio includes speech and music, and the two benefit from different ways of representing sound. A single codec also needs to work across different bandwidths, frame durations, and network conditions.
tldr.mechanism: Opus combines a Linear Prediction layer based on SILK with a Modified Discrete Cosine Transform layer based on CELT. A packet's table-of-contents byte identifies its mode and configuration, while the two layers can operate separately or together.
tldr.outcome: Opus covers narrowband speech through fullband stereo music and can change modes without renegotiating the session. RFC 6716 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8251.

today: RFC 6716 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8251. The decoder reference code in Appendix A is its primary normative definition.

sections.title: Why Opus Uses Two Coding Methods
sections.content:
RFC 6716 defines Opus, an interactive speech and audio codec for uses such as Voice over IP, videoconferencing, in-game chat, and live, distributed music. It combines a layer based on Linear Prediction (LP) with one based on the Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT).

The RFC explains why it combines them: LP methods encode low speech frequencies efficiently, while transform methods work better for music and higher speech frequencies. Using both gives Opus a wider operating range than either method alone, and lets it combine the two in one mode.

The decoder source code in Appendix A is the primary normative definition. Only the decoder portion of that source is normative; the RFC's prose explains the design and its rationale.
sections.plainLanguage: Opus combines two ways to compress sound because speech and music have different patterns. Its decoder's reference code in Appendix A defines the required behavior.

sections.title: Modes, Bandwidths, and Controls
sections.content:
Opus can use the LP layer alone, the MDCT layer alone, or both in Hybrid mode. The LP layer supports narrowband, medium-band, and wideband audio with frame durations from 10 to 60 ms. The MDCT layer supports narrowband through fullband audio with frame durations from 2.5 to 20 ms. Hybrid mode combines them for super-wideband or fullband audio: LP handles frequencies up to 8 kHz, and MDCT handles the higher frequencies.

The RFC gives a bitrate range from 6 kbit/s narrowband mono speech to 510 kbit/s fullband stereo music, and algorithmic delay from 5 ms to 65.2 ms. Opus can switch modes without renegotiating the session. Encoder controls include bitrate, channel count, bandwidth, frame duration, complexity, loss resilience, forward error correction, bitrate mode, and discontinuous transmission. Their effects are signaled in the bitstream, so a decoder does not need separate signaling for those choices.

Frames can last 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 40, or 60 ms, and a packet can combine frames to carry up to 120 ms of audio. Longer packets reduce transport-header overhead, but increase latency and the amount of audio affected by one lost packet. The RFC says 20 ms frames are a good choice for most applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Opus can encode speech, music, or both with two coding methods working together. The sender can change the sound quality, channels, and frame duration while the stream continues. A packet can hold several frames, but longer packets add delay and put more audio at risk if one packet is lost.

sections.title: How Opus Packets Describe Their Frames
sections.content:
An Opus packet is a continuous set of bytes intended to travel as one unit. It can contain multiple frames when they share the same mode, bandwidth, frame duration, and channel count. The framing is not self-delimiting: a lower layer such as UDP or RTP must provide the packet length. The usual framing is required for decoders; the self-delimiting variant in Appendix B is optional.

Every well-formed packet starts with a one-byte table of contents (TOC). Its five-bit configuration identifies the mode, audio bandwidth, and frame duration; a bit identifies mono or stereo; and two bits select how the packet's frame count is represented. The four frame-count codes mean one frame, two equal-sized frames, two differently sized frames, or a signaled number of frames.

Packets with variable-size frames carry lengths for the frames that cannot be inferred from the packet size. A frame cannot exceed 1275 bytes, and a code 3 packet cannot contain more than 120 ms of audio. Its optional padding is added at the Opus layer; encoders must fill the padding bytes with zero. Receivers must not treat packets that violate the framing rules as normal Opus packets; they may discard them as malformed.
sections.plainLanguage: The first byte tells the decoder which Opus settings and frame-count format the packet uses. The packet can then hold one or more compressed audio frames. A receiver must reject packets that break the RFC's framing rules as normal Opus audio.

sections.title: The Decoder Combines Two Layers
sections.content:
The decoder first uses a shared range decoder to read coded symbols. It sends the decoded information to the SILK decoder, the CELT decoder, or both, according to the packet configuration. It converts the layers' outputs to the requested sample rate, aligns their timing, and adds them when both are active.

Both layers use the same range coder, so their data share one coded stream without padding between layers. The coder uses integer arithmetic that must produce exact results. CELT also uses raw bits packed from the end of a frame; these can overlap bytes read ahead by the range decoder, so a decoder must handle that overlap.

The output sample rate can differ from the rate used to encode the audio. The LP layer is resampled to the requested output rate. The MDCT layer operates internally at 48 kHz and can be decimated for lower output rates.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet label tells the decoder which sound layers to run. The decoder converts their output to the requested playback rate and combines the layers when both are active. Both layers share one exact, integer-based data reader.

sections.title: SILK Reconstructs Speech
sections.content:
The LP layer uses a modified version of SILK. It reads parameters from the range-coded stream, builds an excitation signal, and passes that signal through long-term and short-term prediction filters to reconstruct the audio. In Hybrid mode, SILK still operates at wideband internally.

A SILK frame can contain multiple smaller frames, and stereo can add a side channel alongside the mid channel. Optional Low Bit-Rate Redundancy (LBRR) frames carry lower-bitrate encodings of earlier audio to help recover from packet loss. When present, these frames come before the regular SILK frames. The decoder converts the mid-side representation back to left and right channels for stereo output.

SILK's prediction approach is suited to the low frequencies common in speech. The SILK version used inside Opus is substantially modified and is not compatible with the stand-alone SILK codec described by its separate specification.
sections.plainLanguage: SILK rebuilds sound by decoding a compact signal and using prediction filters to shape it. It is suited to speech and can include a reduced-rate copy of earlier audio to help with packet loss. For stereo, the decoder separates the encoded mid and side signals into left and right output.

sections.title: CELT Encodes Frequency Bands
sections.content:
The MDCT layer uses CELT. It divides the sound spectrum into bands that roughly follow the ear's critical frequency bands. CELT encodes each band's energy separately from its spectral shape, which helps preserve the overall energy pattern. In Hybrid mode, it leaves out the bands below 8 kHz because SILK handles those frequencies.

CELT encodes energy in a coarse step followed by two fine steps. It predicts energy from earlier frames and nearby frequency bands, but an intra frame can encode energy without relying on earlier frames. The encoder and decoder derive most of the bit allocation from the packet's available capacity instead of listing every band's allocation. The decoder must reproduce that allocation exactly or the decoded output becomes corrupted.

CELT handles brief transients with several shorter transforms or by changing time-frequency resolution. It also supports mid-side, intensity, and dual stereo coding. A pre-filter and post-filter can improve the treatment of highly tonal and periodic signals.
sections.plainLanguage: CELT divides sound into frequency bands and records each band's loudness and sound pattern. It derives how many bits each band gets from the available packet space, so encoder and decoder must make the same calculation. CELT also has methods for brief sounds and stereo audio.

sections.title: Handling Lost Audio and Mode Changes
sections.content:
Packet Loss Concealment (PLC) is an optional decoder feature that the RFC says should be included for unreliable channels. It is not part of the bitstream, so implementations can choose different quality and complexity trade-offs. The reference decoder repeats a pitch-aligned waveform in CELT mode and extrapolates the signal with linear prediction in SILK mode.

Opus can also include Forward Error Correction (FEC): it encodes selected important speech information again at a lower bitrate and places it in a later packet. SILK's LBRR frames provide this kind of earlier-audio information. A receiver can use concealment when endpoint clocks drift, or skip a packet when the sender's clock runs faster.

Mode and bandwidth changes need care because decoder state and transform overlap affect the sound at the boundary. Some transitions are smoothed by CELT's overlap. Other transitions may include an extra 5 ms CELT frame as redundancy, placed in the frame before or after the change. The RFC specifies those transitions and says not to use PLC during them unless a packet was actually lost.
sections.plainLanguage: If a packet goes missing, the decoder can estimate the missing sound or use a lower-rate copy carried in a later packet. Opus also manages changes between coding modes so the change is less likely to create an audible interruption. Some changes use an extra short CELT frame to smooth the boundary.

sections.title: Encoder Choices and Flexibility
sections.content:
Unlike a decoder, a valid Opus encoder does not have to support every mode; it can contain only a SILK or only a CELT encoder. In the reference encoder, the application chooses the frame duration. Unless the application overrides them, the encoder chooses channel count, bandwidth, and mode based on the requested bitrate, input sample rate, signal type, and frame duration. The application currently supplies the speech-or-music signal type.

The reference encoder converts the input sample rate for SILK and converts stereo input to an adaptive mid-side representation. It analyzes the signal and selects prediction, quantization, and bit-allocation parameters. The CELT encoder makes choices about how to distribute bits among bands and how to code stereo and time-frequency resolution.

The RFC describes encoder controls that can be changed during normal operation without interrupting the audio stream. The choices affect the encoder; their effects are carried in the bitstream so a decoder can decode the stream without out-of-band configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: An Opus encoder can support all modes or only one of the two coding layers. The reference encoder chooses settings such as bandwidth and channel count from the input and requested bitrate, unless the application sets them directly. The decoder learns the selected settings from the audio stream.

sections.title: What a Compliant Decoder Must Match
sections.content:
RFC 6716 defines decoder conformance mainly through the reference implementation in Appendix A. If the prose and the reference code disagree, the code takes precedence. A compliant decoder must produce output within the thresholds of the opus_compare tool for the specified test vectors and for each output rate and channel count it supports. Its final range-decoder state must also match the reference decoder's state.

A decoder does not have to support every output sample rate or channel count. The RFC describes five supported test rates: 8000, 12000, 16000, 24000, and 48000 Hz, and one or two output channels. The comparison tool reports a quality metric: 0 is the pass threshold and 100 means output identical to the reference. For 48 kHz decoding, the RFC recommends a score above 90.

Opus Custom is optional and intended for special sample rates or frame sizes outside the main specification. It uses only CELT and requires out-of-band signaling, so streams using it cannot be expected to decode in every Opus implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: A decoder conforms when its output is close enough to the reference decoder and its range-decoder state matches. It can support only some of the listed playback rates and channel counts. The optional Opus Custom format needs separate signaling and is not supported by every Opus decoder.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns against using Opus with insecure ciphers or cipher modes that are vulnerable to known-plaintext attacks. Opus padding contains zeros, silence frames produce predictable compressed data, and the TOC byte may have a predictable value.

Decoders must handle malicious packets without reading beyond allocated memory or consuming excessive resources. The same concern applies to encoders that process malicious audio, such as in transcoding gateways. On some processors, silence or near-silence can cause slow denormalized floating-point operations; the RFC recommends small offsets or configuring hardware to treat those values as zero when this is a problem.

The RFC reports that its reference implementation had no known buffer overflow or specially crafted input that significantly increased CPU load. It was tested with valid packets, randomly corrupted packets, random packets, and packets from a fuzzing encoder under Valgrind, with no reported errors.
sections.plainLanguage: A decoder must safely handle packets that an attacker has changed or created. It must not read outside its memory or spend excessive resources decoding them. The RFC also warns that predictable codec data should not be used with vulnerable encryption.
